drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6 is one tempo from Rb8+, and with your king headed to d8 that check has real bite. Kd8 walks straight into it: Rb8+ forces Nc8, shoving your knight to a passive square, and then c6 lets White's c5-d6-e6 pawn chain roll forward while the rook swings toward h7 - you went from being better to being lost in four moves. Kc8 sidesteps the check altogether, so the knight stays free on e7 to help contain the pawns instead of hiding on c8. When three connected passers are running, get your king off the checking lines before anything else.
drills.threat: White's rook on b6 wants Rb8+, and your knight on e7 is the only piece that can block that check.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: Your pawn on c5 is hanging, and because your king is still on c8, Rb6xc5 would even come with check along the c-file - White wants that pawn. Kd7 does nothing about it: it just steps off the c-file, and White simply plays Rxc5 for free, then follows with e6+ and Kd8, and you're down real material for nothing, a 3-pawn swing. Nxd5 instead grabs a pawn back immediately, and after Rxc5+ Rc7 Rbc6 Rxc6 Nxc6 the pieces trade down and material stays level. When a pawn's hanging, look for the move that either defends it or wins something back, not one that just relocates your king.
drills.threat: Your c5 pawn is undefended, and White's rook on b6 can grab it with check while your king sits on c8.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king is completely boxed in: the rook on h1 blocks its own escape square, your rook on f2 seals f1, and h2 is only a queen move away from being covered too - White's king has nowhere to run. Rxb2 grabs a pawn but ignores all of that, sending the queen off to the side and letting White scramble with Nd2, Qc2, Rh2, and Qxd3, clawing back a big chunk of your advantage even though you were completely winning. Qg2 was mate on the spot: the queen lands next to the king, defended by your rook on f2, with every flight square covered. When the enemy king's this hemmed in, always scan for a check before reaching for a free pawn.
drills.threat: White's king on g1 has no escape squares left - his own rook on h1 blocks one corner and your rook on f2 covers f1.

Qf3 instead joins the bishop on the attack, keeping the pressure on White's king while you still hold the option of doubling rooks with Rd1 and Rde8. When you've already got a piece aimed at the enemy king, look for ways to add to the attack before playing a purely defensive move.
drills.threat: Your bishop on e5 already sits on the long diagonal aimed straight at White's king on h2 - it just needs backup.

drills.coachNote: You're up a bishop with connected passed pawns rolling - this position wins itself if your king stays on the most useful square, and Black's king on e7 is just hoping for a moment to get active. Kf4 heads toward the kingside pawns but takes the king off its central post, and Black answers with Kf7, e4, Ke7, forcing you to shuffle back with Ke3 to get organized again - you gave back a huge chunk of your advantage without losing anything concrete, just tempo and precision. Kf3 keeps the king centralized and ready to support an e3-e4 break, so Black's king has nothing to latch onto. Even in a completely winning endgame, keep your king on its best square rather than committing it early.

drills.coachNote: Black's king wants to race back to d8 to blockade your c6 pawn before you can walk your own king over to escort it home. Bb3 looks like it does the same job as Ba2, but it doesn't - the line shows you playing Ke7, Kc4, Kf7 and then having to retreat the bishop to a2 anyway, handing Black's king a free tempo in that race. Ba2 does the defensive work immediately, so your king can go straight Kc4-Kb5-Ka6 while Black's king can't catch up. You still won, but you turned an easy, fast win into a much longer grind. In pawn races, don't move a piece to a square you'll have to leave again.

drills.title: vs osmanahma (728) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's rook on f2 and queen on g5 are both bearing down on your knight on d2, and your king on e1 is the piece that pays if it falls. Rf1 doesn't defend d2 or remove either attacker, so Qxd2+ simply wins: your king can't recapture because the rook on f2 still covers d2, and there's no escape square since f1 is now blocked by your own rook. That's mate, turning a position where you were comfortably up material into an instant loss. Qd7+ instead forces Black's king to move first, buying you the tempo to castle queenside next and tuck your king away safely. When your king is this exposed, deal with the checks and threats against it before playing a quiet move like Rf1.
drills.threat: Your knight on d2 is attacked by both Black's rook on f2 and queen on g5, and your king on e1 has nowhere to run.

drills.coachNote: Black's rook on h5 is sitting completely undefended, and his king still hasn't castled off e8 - a check landing on the a2-g8 diagonal hits both problems at once. Qd4 doesn't touch either weakness, so Black gets to play ...Qd7 and start untangling, and a few moves later even lands ...Qa4+ on you, eating into your edge. Qg6+ is the move that cashes in: it forces ...Kd7, since nothing else covers the check, and then Qxh5 simply wins the rook outright because nothing guards it. A couple of moves later you're not just better, you're up a full rook for free. When a piece is sitting undefended, look first for the check or capture that wins it before playing a quiet move.
drills.threat: Black's rook on h5 has no defender at all, and his king still hasn't castled off e8.

drills.coachNote: White's a6 and b6 pawns are only a couple of pushes from queening, and your rook is the only piece that can get behind them and stop the race. Rc4+ gives check, but all it really does is push White's king to d5 - exactly where it wants to go to shepherd the pawns - so you've spent a move helping your opponent's plan along. After Kd5, Rc3, b7, Rb3, White's rook cuts yours off from ever getting behind the pawns and they just keep running. Rc1 does the useful thing instead: after b7, Re1+ forces the king to move, and then Rb1 lands your rook directly behind the pawn where it can actually blockade. Save checks for when they gain you something - here it just handed White a free tempo.

drills.title: vs debaser7 (798) — Slav Defense
drills.coachNote: White's rook on e6 is babysitting the a-pawn's march to a8, and the only way to stop it is to get your own rook directly onto that file. Rc7 sits one file to the side, so it isn't actually in the pawn's way - White just plays b6 and then b7, gaining two free tempi while your rook scrambles from c7 to c1 to a1 before it's finally on the right file, by which point the pawn has already run. Ra7 does the job immediately: it pins the pawn down, forces White to spend a move covering it with Re8, and buys you time to activate your king and rook for counterplay like the later Rg8+. Get your rook onto the passed pawn's file right away, not just nearby.
drills.threat: White's rook on e6 is babysitting the a-pawn's march toward a8, and only a rook on that same file can stop it.

drills.coachNote: Black's bishop is free to swing to g4 and then h3, hunting for ways to harass your kingside pawns while you walk your king in to help finish the game. Kc6 doesn't get in the way of that plan and doesn't make real progress of its own, and the line drifts into Kd6, Kf8, Re7 - still winning, but far slower and messier than it needs to be, which is why the evaluation drops so sharply even though you went on to win. Kb4 instead heads toward c5 first, meeting Black's counterplay before continuing the march with Kd8, Kd6, Kc8. When you're completely winning, every king move should either shut down your opponent's plan or advance yours - not just shuffle.

Rb2 right away gets the rook off the exposed b-file and onto a useful square, letting your king sidestep any harassment with Ka3 next and keep marching in with Kc6. That's mate, flipping a position where you were clearly better into an instant loss. Qh7 keeps f8 covered by offering the trade of queens instead; after Qxh7+ Kxh7, Bf4 Re8 Rxe8 you head into an endgame where you're still doing fine. Ke5 walks your king toward the pawns that actually matter instead: Kc2 Kf4 Kd3 a5 Ke2 keeps you pressing on the side where the danger lives. When your opponent's only hope is a pawn break on one wing, send your king there to smother it rather than drifting toward the other side.

Nbd7 develops a piece but doesn't challenge that center at all, so White gets e5 for free: your knight retreats to e8, Qe2 comes, and you're pushed back with f6, stuck behind White's wall with nothing to show for it. e6-e5 was the moment to strike instead, hitting d4 directly — after e5 dxe5 Ng4 Qf4 Qe7 Nf3 your pieces get active and the center opens for you too. Against a big pawn center, hit it before it hits you.
drills.threat: White's e4-pawn, backed by c4 and d4, is one push from e5 — that would kick your knight on f6 and lock down huge space.

Nd2 was the move: it steps the knight off that diagonal while staying active, and after Nd2 Rd8 Nf3 Kg7 Qc2 Rd6 the position stays level. A queen with a clear diagonal onto one of your pieces is worth a glance before you play a quiet developing move like Rac1.

Re2 avoids the tactic entirely, and after Re2 Qd5 Qf4 Qg5+ Qxg5 Bxg5 you trade into a calmer endgame instead of bleeding more material. A pawn guarded by a queen with a rook stacked behind it isn't free — check who else is watching that square first.

Rf6 was the move to play first, adding pressure before committing the knight; the same Nd2 idea still works later (Rf6 Rfe1 Re8 Rab1 Nd2), just without gifting White a tempo to attack it. An outpost only helps once the piece landing there can't just be kicked for free.

drills.coachNote: White's Nf7 is forking your queen on d8 and rook on h8, and your king on d7 has nowhere calm to sit. Nd5 doesn't defend either target, so Qd6+ forces Ke8 and then Qxd8+ wins your queen — you were up a mountain of material at -4.8, and this handed most of it back. Qg8 was the fix: it saves the queen outright and just accepts Nxh8, Qxh8 as the cost, then c4, c5, O-O-O lets you finish developing with your king safe and still a winning material edge. When a knight forks two pieces, save the more valuable one and write off the rest.

drills.coachNote: White's knight on e4 wants to hop into d6 with check, forking your king on e8 and hitting toward f7 and c8. Bd6 walks right into it — Nxd6+ wins the bishop outright, and after Ke7, the other knight jumps in with Nf7, forking your queen on d8 and rook on h8, so you're forced into Qe8 with your king stuck on e7 and most of your -3.8 edge gone. Bf8 sidesteps the fork entirely, tucking the bishop home and keeping castling rights alive, so after Bd3, Qb6, Nxe6, Ne5, Nxg7+ you're meeting White's tactics from solid footing instead of scrambling. Get your king safe before two enemy knights get to aim at the same fork square.

drills.coachNote: Once a black rook lands on c8, it skewers your rook on c7 and the knight sitting behind it on c6 — you're going to lose tempo untangling that no matter what. Rxc7 grabs a pawn but ignores this: Rec8 forces Rxc8+, Rxc8, and now your knight on c6 is attacked again with no rook to shield it, so you burn another move retreating to Nd4 while Black's rook sits active on c8. g4 leaves the c7 pawn alone and starts your own kingside play instead — after Rac8, Rd5 centralizes, and Re6, Rc5, Ke8 keeps you dictating events rather than reacting. In an ending, a free pawn isn't worth it if it hands over several moves of initiative.
